video_title: How to Play the Money Game | TCAF 256
gist: CNBC's Michael Santoli joins Josh Brown and Michael Batnick for a wide-ranging conversation on why prediction demand outstrips forecasting skill, why Treasury yields are rising for structural (not credit) reasons, how mechanical/programmatic flows are driving 'immaculate rotation' inside a historically concentrated market, and why AI capex spending, retail behavior, and current valuations echo (but don't exactly repeat) prior speculative eras from the 1968 'Money Game' mainframe boom to the 2020 Tesla melt-up.

insights.claim: The public's psychological demand for market predictions is what generates the supply of confident forecasts on financial TV and in newsletters, regardless of anyone's actual ability to see the future — so a pundit's willingness to make a call says more about audience demand than forecasting edge.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Discount on-air conviction calls as demand-driven content rather than genuine signal; weight track records and admitted uncertainty more than confident predictions.
insights.quote: The demand being there, the the predictions must be supplied.

insights.claim: Santoli's years-long anonymous-source device, the 'mystery broker' (a financial adviser who called the 2007 top and then declared the financial crisis over later in 2009), shows how a small, unverifiable track record combined with mystique can become durable market lore that readers obsess over even though the person is, in Santoli's words, 'nobody you've heard of.'
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Treat cult 'guru' indicators skeptically — their popularity reflects narrative appeal, not statistically reliable edge.

insights.claim: Stock pundits are increasingly held to a harsher, sports-betting-style standard than NFL commentators, and that gap in accountability is intensifying as retail brokerages (Robinhood) and platforms like Interactive Brokers add prediction markets, blurring the line between investing commentary and gambling picks.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Expect louder, more personal backlash against high-profile stock calls going forward, and growing convergence between prediction-market products and equity trading platforms.

insights.claim: A golf pro quoted in an FT story on meme-stock trading explained he preferred buying deeply distressed, binary-risk stocks like bankrupt Hertz over sports betting because a losing stock bet ('down 30%') still leaves 70% of capital intact, versus a losing sports bet that wipes out the full stake — illustrating retail investors' flawed but intuitive risk framing around equities as safer 'gambling.'
insights.speaker: guest, recounting an FT anecdote
insights.so_what: Watch for retail piling into high-volatility, distressed or bankrupt names on the mistaken belief that equity's 'partial loss' structure makes it inherently less risky than binary bets.

insights.claim: Permabear commentators tend to abandon a falsified thesis and rotate to a new bearish argument rather than concede the market proved them wrong (e.g., 2024 concentration fears in the Mag 7 were quietly dropped once the market broadened, replaced by fresh concerns about the national debt), while bulls more consistently acknowledge downside risks exist even as they stay long.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host; agreed by Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Treat persistent, goalpost-shifting bearish narratives with more skepticism than persistent bullish ones, since markets rise roughly 70% of years and 55% of days.

insights.claim: A stock is inert paper with no memory of an investor's purchase price or feelings toward it — psychological attachment (love for a winner, anchoring to cost basis, revenge trading after a loss) is entirely one-sided and, per the 1968 book The Money Game, can curdle into self-destructive investing behavior.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest, reading from The Money Game
insights.so_what: A durable behavioral checkpoint: if a decision is driven by attachment to a name or a cost basis rather than forward-looking fundamentals, it's a signal to reassess.
insights.quote: The stock doesn't know you own it.

themes.theme: Rates, Fiscal Backdrop & the 2026 Yield Story

insights.claim: Rising Treasury yields in 2026 reflect the bond market having to 'reprice and ration' an unusually large global demand for capital — driven by roughly $1.7 trillion in annual corporate debt issuance (about 30% more than the prior year, much of it AAA-rated) competing directly with Treasuries for the same buyer base — rather than any deterioration in US creditworthiness.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Rising yields here are a supply/demand-for-capital story, not a credit-quality sell signal — don't read higher rates as the market pricing default risk.
insights.quote: The world is demanding so much capital the bond market has to repric and ration it, right?

insights.claim: The 2026 rise in long-term yields is driven by several simultaneous, largely independent forces — chronic political dysfunction, a global (not just US-specific) rise in long-bond yields, record corporate debt supply, and inflation that is sticky-to-rising — so no single narrative fully explains the move.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host; confirmed by Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Avoid single-cause explanations for the 2026 rate backdrop when constructing a fixed-income or duration view — treat it as a multi-factor regime.

insights.claim: US interest expense has climbed back to roughly 3% of GDP, a level last reached in the early 1990s, when it helped fuel Ross Perot's single-issue third-party presidential campaign centered on the debt and trade — and arguably contributed, alongside political gridlock, to the fiscal discipline that produced a budget surplus by the late 1990s.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Rising interest-expense-to-GDP has historically been a political flashpoint that can force fiscal discipline — watch for a similar political response as debt-service costs climb.
insights.quote: we're basically at 3% of GDP goes to paying interest on the debt.

insights.claim: Santoli argues an AI-driven productivity 'miracle' may not replicate the 1990s economic benefit as cleanly because the two eras' starting conditions differ: in the 1990s, debt-to-GDP was steadily falling toward a surplus and there were far fewer retirees per working person, whereas today's AI buildout is occurring against high, rising debt and adverse demographics.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Temper expectations that AI-driven productivity gains will show up in the same GDP/fiscal way the 1990s tech boom did — the debt and demographic base case is structurally worse.

insights.claim: Santoli frames chronic US fiscal deficit concern as an 'underlying autoimmune condition' — usually dormant, but flaring into visible symptoms (bond-market scares, political panic) under acute stress, even though the structural condition itself hasn't necessarily worsened suddenly.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Use this model to distinguish a genuine fiscal regime change from a temporary flare-up in bond-vigilante sentiment before repositioning around debt fears.

insights.claim: President Trump's public argument that the US deserves the world's lowest interest rates because of strong economic performance reflects a real-estate/casino borrower's mental model (lower rates as a reward for doing well), which is the inverse of how bond traders actually price debt — strong growth signals a future need to tighten money supply, which pushes yields up, not down.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host, analyzing a Trump video clip
insights.so_what: Don't expect political rhetoric framing strong growth as grounds for rate cuts to match how the bond market will actually respond to strong growth data.

insights.claim: What looks like an 'immaculate rotation' between sectors (semis down 2% offset by Apple up and healthcare rallying on the same day) is largely mechanical, programmatic factor-neutralizing flow from market-making hedge funds like Jane Street, Susquehanna, and Citadel — not traders actively reacting to news.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli and Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Don't over-interpret same-day cross-sector moves as fundamental signal — much of it is systematic hedging/rebalancing flow with no informational content.

insights.claim: There has been no 'all or nothing' trading day (where essentially every S&P 500 stock moves in the same direction) since December 31, 2025 — the longest such streak since 2001 — reflecting how concentrated, offsetting factor trades between AI/semis and the rest of the market have replaced broad single-direction market days.
insights.speaker: hosts, citing Bespoke data
insights.so_what: The absence of unified market-wide moves is itself a market-structure indicator of extreme sector offsetting/concentration, useful for gauging systemic fragility.
insights.quote: We haven't had that since December 31st, 2025. That's the longest streak. Since 2001.

insights.claim: Energy stocks became the market's consensus 'negative beta' diversifier in 2026 largely because bonds no longer reliably hedge equities and traditional defensive proxies like utilities have themselves become AI-capex-linked (and thus positively correlated) trades — but Santoli cautions this diversifier role is a byproduct of the current setup, not a structural property of energy stocks.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Don't assume energy will keep behaving as a portfolio diversifier once the current AI-driven correlation regime shifts — the negative beta is situational, not permanent.

insights.claim: In a genuine macro shock, systematic/algorithmic market-making strategies 'turn off' or step away first rather than continue trading normally — so the appearance of orderly, mechanical rotation in calm conditions shouldn't be taken as evidence the market would stay liquid and orderly during a real crisis.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: A useful risk-management caveat: current mechanical liquidity/rotation is a fair-weather phenomenon, not proof the market can absorb a genuine shock without a liquidity air-pocket.

insights.claim: Santoli's history covering post-1987-crash NYSE 'program trading' reports shows the definition of what counted as a 'program' was arbitrary and shifted with the exchange's PR incentives — understated in the 1990s to avoid looking bot-driven, then emphasized from the early 2000s onward to look 'high-tech' — a caution that widely-cited market-structure statistics can reflect institutional narrative more than rigorous methodology.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Apply the same skepticism to today's headline market-structure statistics (HFT share, program-trading volume) — definitions can be as much marketing as measurement.

insights.claim: Retail investors bought the most tech stocks in five weeks even as semiconductor and DRAM names got hit during a Korea-related leverage/'situational' unwind, continuing to pile into semis via vehicles like a DRAM ETF while institutional flow pulled back — showing retail is currently the dominant, largely price-insensitive marginal buyer in AI/semi names.
insights.speaker: hosts, citing a chart shared by John Authers
insights.so_what: Retail flow is currently propping up semiconductor/AI names on dips; a reversal in retail sentiment could remove an important marginal bid under the sector.

insights.claim: Retail investors structurally 'don't crystallize losses' — they tend to hold underwater positions expecting mean reversion rather than sell, which biases aggregate retail flow toward persistent net buying except when forced out by margin calls, unlike the more semi-professional trader base that uses platforms like Interactive Brokers.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Retail-heavy names may show unusually 'sticky' downside (slow to capitulate) compared to institutionally-owned names — relevant for gauging capitulation risk in high-retail-ownership stocks.

insights.claim: Per Vanguard's own data, 401(k) investors did not sell during the COVID crash and in fact bought 'every print on the way down' — making this largely passive, forced-savings cohort arguably the best-performing investor class in the country, outperforming more actively managed money simply by not reacting.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Michael Batnick, citing Vanguard
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case for automatic, behaviorally-insulated retirement-account investing over discretionary trading during drawdowns.

insights.claim: Citadel flow strategist Scott Rubner tracks retail net selling as a rare, high-signal contrarian indicator — retail was a net seller in the last week of March 2026, which coincided with the market bottom, and again in the last week of July 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest, citing Scott Rubner
insights.so_what: Weeks when retail turns a net seller (a rare event) have historically clustered near short-term market lows — worth tracking as a tactical buy-the-dip signal.

insights.claim: The explosive growth of covered-call/options-income ETFs (e.g., NEO/Innovator products, both recently acquired by Goldman Sachs) reflects retail demand for defined-outcome, capped-upside/limited-downside exposure — Santoli calls them 'private social security' since many buyers use the option premium income to fund retirement-like cash flow, a category that didn't meaningfully exist before because equities never let investors pre-select a specific risk/reward range.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Covered-call/income ETF flows are now large enough to matter for index option positioning and realized volatility — a structural, sticky source of options supply to monitor.
insights.quote: the options income funds are like private social security

insights.claim: The S&P 500 hit roughly 23x forward earnings last October (2025) on what were then near-peak earnings; since then earnings have grown faster than the index price, compressing the forward multiple even though the index itself is higher — so today's 'cheaper' valuation started from an already elevated base.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: The apparent multiple compression is real but shouldn't be read as the market having become cheap in absolute terms.

insights.claim: On a forward price-to-free-cash-flow basis, the S&P 500 trades near 30x — a much more stretched multiple than the headline forward P/E suggests, because capex-heavy AI-driven growth is consuming free cash flow that historically flowed to buybacks and dividends.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Investors relying solely on P/E to judge valuation are missing that the market is materially more expensive on a free-cash-flow basis due to the capex supercycle.

insights.claim: Big Tech's declining free cash flow from AI capex is a deliberate, disclosed management choice — not an involuntary drag — as executives who studied Amazon's shareholder letters and 'grew up worshiping Jeff Bezos' knowingly sacrifice near-term FCF for long-term positioning, and Wall Street is tolerating the trade-off, at least for now, because it recognizes the intent.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Judge AI-capex-heavy companies by whether the market's patience with negative FCF persists, not by FCF alone — a shift in investor tolerance would be a real catalyst.

insights.claim: Santoli sees genuine, revealed demand behind the AI infrastructure buildout (not pure speculation), but flags a structural risk that 'capitalism shouldn't work' when numerous large companies simultaneously spend all their free cash flow chasing the same opportunity, since that dynamic makes it unlikely everyone involved earns a strong return.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Expect a shakeout among AI-capex spenders even if the underlying technology thesis proves correct — simultaneous overbuilding rarely rewards every participant.

insights.claim: Historically, stocks doing the biggest buybacks were not disproportionately 'goosed' by them, undercutting the popular claim that buybacks mechanically inflate share prices — but buybacks do serve a real function by offsetting dilution from heavy stock-based compensation at large tech companies, effectively monetizing employee equity comp without net shareholder dilution.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Don't treat aggregate buyback dollars as a bullish price catalyst on their own — their real economic role is dilution offset, not price support.

insights.claim: Santoli's own written framework for approaching the current bull market is that it is 'prudent to assume the valuation peak is in' and then be open to a pleasant surprise if that assumption proves wrong — i.e., default to caution on further multiple expansion rather than betting on it.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: A concrete positioning heuristic: plan portfolios assuming no further multiple expansion, treating any additional re-rating as upside optionality rather than a base case.
insights.quote: Prudent to assume that the valuation peak is in then be open to pleasant surprise if not.

insights.claim: Current S&P 500 profit margins near 15% despite revenue growth of only about 4% this quarter reflect compositional shift — the largest index constituents are increasingly higher-margin, business-to-business capital-goods companies (semis, hyperscalers) rather than the consumer-facing names people intuitively associate with 'the economy,' so headline margin strength doesn't necessarily indicate broad economic health.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Don't extrapolate S&P margin/earnings strength to the health of the broader consumer economy — the index composition has shifted toward capital-goods suppliers.

insights.claim: The current generation of S&P 500 CEOs and CFOs may be the most 'battle-tested' cohort in modern corporate history, having navigated first-term Trump tariffs and public attacks, COVID, January 6th, retail culture-war backlash, second-term 'Liberation Day' tariffs, the Iran war, and elevated inflation in rapid succession — plausible institutional resilience that helps explain persistently high margins despite the shock sequence.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host; agreed by Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Corporate management quality/resilience is an underappreciated tailwind for margin durability that isn't captured in standard macro models.

insights.claim: Micron's market capitalization is roughly 10 times that of Disney, yet public perception of 'how's the economy doing' still anchors to consumer-facing names like Disney or Target rather than to industrial/AI-supply-chain names like Micron — even though Micron-type companies are what's actually driving current S&P earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host
insights.so_what: Popular economic sentiment and what's actually moving the index's earnings can diverge sharply — don't use consumer-brand anecdotes as a proxy for index-level earnings health.
insights.quote: Micron is 10 times bigger than Disney.

themes.theme: AI Capex Bubble Signals & Historical Parallels

insights.claim: Santoli reads a 1968 passage from Adam Smith's The Money Game describing 1960s investors' euphoric extrapolation of mainframe-computer-leasing earnings ('will double next year, will double again the year after') as an explicit parallel to today's AI infrastructure narrative — while noting the underlying mainframe computing revolution was, in fact, real, just as AI's long-run technology thesis may also prove real even if near-term stock extrapolation is excessive.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest, reading from The Money Game
insights.so_what: Real technology revolutions and overextended near-term stock extrapolation can and do coexist — being right about the technology doesn't guarantee current prices are justified.
insights.quote: Therefore earnings will be up 100% this year will double next year. We'll double again the year after that. The surface has barely been scratched. The rise has scarcely begun.

insights.claim: Santoli's 'everything ends in a boring place' thesis: every exciting growth story, if successful, eventually matures into a low-multiple, utility-like business — his examples being eBay (moonshot to mature marketplace) and stablecoin issuer Circle (essentially a spread-earning bond custodian analogous to Bank of New York Mellon, which trades around 12x earnings) — so investors should plan for how today's exciting AI-linked names 'decelerate' into ordinary companies.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Model current high-growth AI-linked names' eventual steady-state multiple and margin profile rather than extrapolating current growth rates indefinitely.
insights.quote: everything ends in a boring place.

insights.claim: Stripe's roughly $7–7.5 billion acquisition of AI-model marketplace Open Router — whose revenue tripled to just $13 million and which had been valued at only $1.3 billion three months earlier in May 2026 — is cited as a live test of whether AI-infrastructure deal valuations are rational, drawing explicit comparison to Meta's WhatsApp and Instagram deals and Apple's Beats purchase, all mocked at the time but later vindicated.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown, host
insights.so_what: Extreme, fast-multiplying private valuations in AI infrastructure could be either a rational land-grab (per the WhatsApp/Instagram/Beats precedent) or a bubble marker — worth tracking as a real-time test case.
insights.quote: Stripe is going to pay 7 to 7.5 billion. The valuation on Open Router in May, which was 3 months ago, was 1.3 billion.

insights.claim: Mainstream investors now casually discuss granular AI supply-chain minutiae (chip yields, wafers, repurposing jet engines into gas-turbine generators for data centers) despite not understanding the underlying technology — per both hosts and Santoli, this kind of widespread technical fluency without real expertise is historically a 'toppy' sentiment signal, echoing prior fads like iPhone-teardown component-basket trades and EV/lithium supply-chain baskets that each faded after roughly a year.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Widespread amateur fluency in a sector's technical jargon is a soft sentiment-exhaustion indicator worth watching alongside more quantitative measures.

insights.claim: Tesla's roughly 3,600% lifetime outperformance versus the S&P 500 is concentrated almost entirely in calendar year 2020 (the stock rose roughly 10x that year alone); since then it has broadly held those gains without adding much further relative outperformance, showing how a single extraordinary year can define a stock's entire multi-year track record.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Be cautious extrapolating a stock's long-run outperformance track record forward when it's actually attributable to one anomalous year rather than sustained compounding.
insights.quote: It's outperform the SP by like what 3600%. It's massive. Every every basis point of the outperformance happened in calendar year 2020.

insights.claim: Western Digital's spinoff of SanDisk about a year and a half ago was initially unwanted by investors, yet SanDisk shares have since risen 'thousands of percent' — reportedly a move shareholders themselves had pushed the company to make — illustrating how an unloved corporate action can become the market's biggest winner.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Spinoffs that the market initially shuns are worth a second look, especially in cyclical/commodity-tech segments like memory chips that can re-rate sharply.
insights.quote: Western Digital spun off SanDisk a year and a half ago.

insights.claim: Santoli treats Elon Musk/Tesla as an exception to the 'everything matures and slows down' rule because Musk actively cannibalizes his own successful products (discontinuing the Model S and Model X in favor of new bets like humanoid robots) rather than letting them decelerate into mature, boring franchises.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Standard 'growth-to-value maturation' valuation frameworks may not apply cleanly to Tesla given Musk's willingness to disrupt his own product lines.

insights.claim: The end of a bear market and the start of a bull market are only ever identifiable in retrospect — despite conventional charting that dates the current secular bull market from the March 2009 low, in real time the post-2008 period was still widely perceived and discussed as merely a bear-market rally through roughly 2012-2013.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli and Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of retrospective bull/bear-market dating conventions when using them to judge current market age or historical analogs — contemporaneous sentiment often disagreed with the eventual chart-based label.

insights.claim: Strategist Byron Wien entered the business in the late 1950s just as stock dividend yields first crossed below Treasury yields — an event that had reliably signaled an overvalued market top before that — yet the market didn't top and instead rose for roughly 50 years until the global financial crisis; older strategists anchored to that 'sell' rule lost clients and never adapted, which reportedly shaped Wien's decision to later publish an annual '10 Surprises' list to actively test his own blind spots.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Rigid rule-of-thumb valuation signals (like dividend-yield-vs-Treasury crossovers) can fail for decades — build humility and self-testing (à la Wien's Surprises list) into any fixed valuation framework.

insights.claim: Outside strategist research cited by Santoli found that broader market participation is not empirically associated with more stable or rewarding markets — in fact, bull markets tend to be where concentration happens, contradicting the popular assumption that a 'broadening' market is inherently healthier than a concentrated one.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Don't treat rising market breadth as an automatic bullish confirmation signal, or narrow leadership as an automatic warning sign — the historical relationship is weaker than commonly assumed.
insights.quote: bull markets are where concentration happens.

insights.claim: Over roughly the past 15 years, the market's typical response to a negative internal divergence (e.g., small caps or value stocks lagging while large-cap growth hits new highs) has almost always been resolved by a 'catch-up' from the lagging segment rather than a 'catch-down' from the leaders, contrary to the common assumption that such divergences must resolve via the broader market falling to meet the laggards.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: When laggard segments (small caps, value) diverge from index leaders, the historical base rate favors positioning for a catch-up rally in the laggards rather than betting on a broad market decline.

insights.claim: The old rule of thumb that '15x earnings is the S&P's long-term fair multiple' was rooted in an economy that cycled through a manufacturing-driven recession roughly every three years with mean-reverting profit margins — a framework Santoli says no longer applies because current margins don't mean-revert the way they historically did.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Retire static historical P/E 'fair value' anchors — the underlying margin-cyclicality assumption they were built on no longer holds in the current economy.

insights.claim: Santoli says he 'only likes the beginnings of things' — rallies born out of skepticism and disbelief — and grows uneasy once a rally becomes self-congratulatory and consensus-driven ('earnings are the lifeblood,' 'I told you not to panic'), but explicitly cautions that this personal discomfort with a maturing narrative is not itself a reason to call a top, since such phases usually 'aren't over' just because they feel overextended.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: A useful check on one's own bearish instincts: a rally 'feeling' tired or consensus-driven is not itself sufficient evidence to reduce exposure.
insights.quote: I only like the beginnings of things.

insights.claim: Santoli predicts he would be 'moderately surprised' if, a year from now, the market is still comfortable with the same narrative of persistent negative free cash flow among AI-capex leaders ('it's coming, it's going to pay off') without either the payoff materializing or an intervening 'scare and relief cycle' gut-check along the way.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: Sets a roughly 12-month checkpoint for whether the market's patience with negative-FCF AI capex spending holds or breaks — a concrete, time-bound thing to monitor.

insights.claim: Despite ongoing Iran-related war tensions and the Strait of Hormuz being closed — a scenario that could plausibly have produced a 'black swan' energy-limit-up/stocks-limit-down event — none of that materialized, and equity indices sit at or near all-time highs; Santoli attributes his lack of surprise to roughly 6% nominal GDP growth and record corporate earnings/margins absorbing the geopolitical and rate risk.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Michael Santoli
insights.so_what: Geopolitical tail risks that fail to materialize into market disruption shouldn't be read as 'proof' such risks don't matter — strong underlying earnings and growth were the actual offsetting force this cycle.

insights.claim: Santoli attributes market strength to a broad 'swing from labor to capital' — corporate earnings and margins are surging even as macro headlines look shaky, because the S&P 500 disproportionately captures a business-to-business, capital-goods-oriented 'wholesale economy' rather than the broader consumer economy that ordinary sentiment surveys track.
insights.speaker: Michael Santoli, guest
insights.so_what: The index's earnings strength is structurally tied to capital-side (not labor-side) economic gains — a useful lens for reconciling strong index performance with softer consumer/labor sentiment data.
